concepts.name: Perfect Pipeline Throughput and Total Cycles
facts: In an ideal five-stage pipeline with no bubbles, one instruction completes per cycle after the pipeline fills, giving a closed-form expression for total cycles and throughput.

A perfect pipeline has no stalls (bubbles), so it achieves maximum throughput. For N instructions executing through an M-stage pipeline, the first instruction takes M cycles to complete, and each subsequent instruction completes one per cycle. Thus Total Cycles = M + N - 1. Average throughput is N / (M + N - 1) instructions per cycle, and the per-second instruction throughput is Frequency * N / (M + N - 1). As N grows large, throughput approaches one instruction per cycle.

concepts.name: Branch Predictability and Speculative Execution Strategies
facts: Branches are predictable, enabling speculative execution; strategies range from naive static prediction (compiler-driven) to dynamic branch prediction that learns behavior autonomously.

Naive speculative execution uses static prediction: the compiler analyzes user code, identifies branches that would not be taken, and removes the corresponding instructions to avoid control hazards. Dynamic branch prediction instead learns branch behavior autonomously without compiler analysis or profiling, and can adapt to changing branch behavior over time. The example illustrates why branches are predictable, motivating speculation as a latency-hiding technique in CPUs.

required_points.text: In an ideal five-stage pipeline with no bubbles, one instruction completes per cycle after the pipeline fills, giving a closed-form expression for total cycles and throughput.

evidence.quote:

      the pipeline.

   ¡ No bubbles and maximum throughput.


¡ For N instructions and M stages:

   ¡  Total Cycles = M + N – 1

   ¡  Average throughput
     = N / (M + N - 1) instructions per cycle

   ¡  Instruction throughput per second
     Frequency * N / (M + N - 1)

required_points.text: A perfect pipeline has no stalls (bubbles), so it achieves maximum throughput. Average throughput is N / (M + N - 1) instructions per cycle, and the per-second instruction throughput is Frequency * N / (M + N - 1). As N grows large, throughput approaches one instruction per cycle.
